# Colors

Figma: [Colors](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-879)

The color system has three layers: primitives are raw color values, semantics name colors by intent (bg/surface, text/default), and themable tokens swap per theme. Always reference semantic tokens in product UI, never primitives directly.

## Color Architecture

### Three Layers

- Primitives - Raw color values. Nine ramps with 10 stops each, plus 3 shades and 8 alpha values. Single mode. Never themed. Designers should not reference these directly in product UI.
- Semantics - Intent-named tokens. bg/surface is "the page background," text/default is "default body text color." Aliases a primitive, two modes (Light/Dark). This is what designers and engineers use.
- Themable - A subset of 24 semantic tokens that swap per theme (Founding Day, Ramadan, partner themes). Everything else stays locked.

## Primitive Ramps

- Ten ramps × ten stops each = 100 primitive color tokens. Each ramp is single-mode (one value across all themes). Use semantic tokens that alias these - not the primitives directly.
- Primary · LightGreen · 50 · #FAFDFB · 100 · #E4F3E5 · 200 · #D6EDD9 · 300 · #AEDAB2 · 400 · #77C27F · 500 · #4DAA57 · 600 · #469B4F · 700 · #387C3F · 800 · #2A5D2F · 900 · #1C3E20

## Shades & Alpha Primitives

- Three solid shades (White, Off-White, Black) and eight alpha primitives. Off-White is Safqah's warm canvas. Alphas are used for scrims, overlays, and disabled treatments.

### Solid Shades

- White · #FFFFFF
- Off-White · #F4F6F2
- Black · #000000

## Semantic Colors

- Intent-named tokens that alias primitives. Two modes (Light/Dark). 24 of these are themable (swap per theme); the rest are locked. This is what designers and engineers reference in product UI.

### Why colors matter

Color is the most immediate signal in any user interface. Before a user reads a word, they perceive the dominant hue, the contrast between text and background, the way emphasis flows across the screen. In financial products like Safqah, color also carries trust - users associate certain palettes with reliability, professionalism, and safety with their money.

A design system's color layer does three jobs at once. First, it ensures consistency: the same green means the same thing across every screen. Second, it ensures accessibility: every color combination meets contrast standards so users with low vision can still operate the product. Third, it ensures flexibility: when Safqah adds a Founding Day theme or partners with another brand, the system swaps colors without breaking anything else.

Without a system, you get drift - the kind of slow inconsistency where every screen feels slightly off from every other screen. Buttons in three slightly different greens. Error messages that don't quite match. Backgrounds that shift tone for no clear reason. The Syntropy color system exists to prevent that drift.

### The 3-layer model

Syntropy organizes color into three layers, each with a clear role. Understanding why each layer exists is the foundation of using the system correctly.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Layer 1 - Primitives | The 90+ raw color values. Nine ramps with 10 stops each, plus 3 shades and 8 alpha values. Single-mode, never themed, and never referenced directly in product UI. Think of them as paint chips - designers don't pick paint chips for a wall, they pick "kitchen wall color," which references a chip. |
| Layer 2 - Semantics | The 113+ intent-named tokens that alias primitives. bg/surface means "the page background." text/default means "default body text." Two values per token (Light + Dark mode). This is the layer designers and engineers reference in their work. |
| Layer 3 - Themable | A subset of 24 semantic tokens that swap per theme. When Safqah runs a Founding Day campaign, only these 24 change - everything else stays locked. This makes seasonal and partner themes possible without rebuilding the system. |

> **Tip:** Mental model: primitives are the materials, semantics are labels you put on materials for specific uses, themable are labels that can swap to a different material when needed.

### Choosing the right token

The most common mistake new designers make is using the wrong token for a given context. Here's how to decide.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| For backgrounds | Start with bg/surface - it's the canvas for content. Use bg/base when you need stronger separation, like inside a modal or card. Use bg/elevated for raised surfaces that need slight differentiation. Never use a primitive color directly for a background. |
| For text | Start with text/default for body content. Use text/muted for supporting text like captions, helper text, or descriptions. Use text/subtle for the least important text like metadata. Use text/disabled only on disabled inputs (disabled elements are exempt from WCAG contrast). |
| For brand emphasis | Use text/brand/darkest for branded text on neutral surfaces (passes AA Normal). Use text/brand/primary only when paired with a visible non-color affordance like a border - it fails AA Normal on its own. Both swap per theme. |
| For status messages | Match the meaning, not the color. Success messages use text/success on bg/success-subtle. Warnings use text/warning on bg/warning-subtle. Don't use a green primitive for "this is good" - use text/success, which means "this conveys success" regardless of what specific green is active. |

> **Tip:** When in doubt, look at the semantic token names. They describe intent, not appearance. Pick the token whose intent matches what you're building, and the system handles the rest.

### Working with brand colors

The Safqah brand is built around a green identity. The Syntropy color system maps that brand into 24 themable tokens - backgrounds, borders, text, icons, and a focus indicator. These are the only tokens that swap per theme.

Within the brand family, you'll see multiple stops (lightest, primary, darkest) and multiple states (default, hover, pressed). This isn't excess - each token has a specific role in interactive UI.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Surface stops | bg/brand/lightest is for subtle branded surfaces like the selected state of a list item. bg/brand/primary is for the main CTA button. bg/brand/darkest is for the strongest emphasis - a hero header background, or a highly emphasized callout. |
| Interactive states | Every primary surface has -hover and -pressed variants. Use them only on actually interactive elements. If a card isn't clickable, don't apply hover states to it - that's a usability lie. |
| The yellow accent | bg/brand/yellow is a secondary brand color. Use sparingly for callouts, highlights, or accent surfaces. Do NOT pair it with brand-green text - that combination fails WCAG. Yellow surfaces use text/default for content text. |

> **Warning:** Never reference Color/Primary/LightGreen/500 or any other primitive color directly in product UI. Always use a semantic token like bg/brand/primary. When themes change, primitives don't - only semantics do.

### Working with status colors

Status colors communicate state: a successful transaction, a warning, an error, a piece of info, a loading process. Syntropy provides six status families: Success (green), Warning (orange), Error (red), Info (blue), Progress (purple), and brown (caution). Each has matching bg, text, border, and icon tokens.

Status colors are intentionally NOT themable. A red error message must look like an error regardless of theme. If Safqah ran a Founding Day theme that changed errors to brown, users would miss the urgency. Status meanings are universal.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Subtle vs filled | Each status has two surface intensities: bg/{status}-subtle (light wash, used for Alert backgrounds and inline status messages) and bg/{status} (filled, used for status badges and emphasized states). Pair subtle backgrounds with text/{status} for body, filled backgrounds with text/on-brand (white) for labels. |
| When to use Progress | Progress (purple) is for "this is happening right now" - loading states, in-progress workflows, things the user is mid-way through. It's distinct from Info (blue) which is for static informational messages. |
| Pairing with icons | Status tokens have matching icon/{status} variants. A success message gets icon/success (the checkmark color). An error gets icon/error. The icon and text use the same hue family so they read as one unit. |

> **Tip:** Be careful not to overload "good things are green" beyond status. The brand green is also green. Distinguishing brand-green from success-green visually is important for clarity.

### WCAG accessibility

WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) defines minimum contrast ratios between text and its background. The standards exist so people with low vision, color blindness, or in difficult viewing conditions (sunlight, low-quality screens) can still read your interface.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| AA Normal - 4.5:1 | The standard threshold for body text below 18px Regular or below 14px Bold. This is what most product text must meet. If text on a background measures 4.5:1 or higher in contrast ratio, it passes. |
| AA Large - 3:1 | A more lenient threshold for larger or bolder text. Applies to text 18px+ Regular or 14px+ Bold. This exists because larger text is inherently easier to read, so it doesn't need as much contrast. |
| AAA - 7:1 | The highest threshold. Aspirational, not required. Some industries (medical, legal) mandate AAA, but most consumer products target AA. Syntropy doesn't require AAA but encourages it where it doesn't hurt design quality. |
Syntropy was verified against AA standards across 74 critical text-on-background pairs. Most pass AA Normal. A small set (11 pairs) fail AA Normal but pass AA Large - these are documented as "Accepted Constraints" with specific usage rules attached.

> **Warning:** Constraint 1 - Button label minimum weight: All buttons with white text on filled brand backgrounds (bg/brand/primary, bg/success, bg/warning, etc.) MUST use 14px+ Bold or 18px+ Regular. Smaller or lighter text fails WCAG.

> **Warning:** Constraint 2 - Brand text requires border affordance: text/brand/primary fails AA Normal on neutral surfaces. Use only when paired with a visible non-color affordance (border, underline, icon). Never for body links - use text/default underlined or text/brand/darkest instead.

> **Warning:** Constraint 3 - Yellow surfaces don't use green text: bg/brand/yellow and bg/brand/yellow-subtle use text/default for content. Brand green colors only for icons or borders on yellow surfaces.

> **Warning:** Constraint 4 - Status text uses /700 stop in Light mode, tuned stops in Dark mode (Green/300, Orange/300, Red/200, Blue/200, Purple/300). This was intentionally tuned for AA Normal compliance on subtle status backgrounds.

### Adding a theme

Themes are how Syntropy adapts to special occasions and partners without rebuilding the system. A Founding Day theme during Saudi National Day. A Ramadan theme during the holy month. A partner co-branding theme. Each only changes the 24 themable tokens - everything else stays locked.

The full theme-adding process is documented in the Stage 2-2 Notion page. Here's the high-level flow.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Step 1 - Add a Semantic mode | In the Figma file, open the Variables panel, find the Semantic collection, add a new mode (e.g., "Founding Day"). The mode goes on the Semantic collection ONLY - never on Primitive Core or Typography. |
| Step 2 - Create a new brand ramp in primitives | Add a new color family in Primitive Core (e.g., Color/Theme-FoundingDay/Sand/50–900). Critical: this is a NEW primitive family, not a modification of existing primitives. Existing values stay locked. |
| Step 3 - Override the 24 themable tokens | For the new mode column in Semantic, set each of the 24 themable tokens to alias the new brand ramp. Use Option B perceptual matching - Light themes use mid-stops, Dark themes shift one stop up. |
| Steps 4–7 - Verify and document | Run the audit pass to confirm no primitive values changed. Run the alias resolver to catch broken references. Run WCAG verification on the new theme. Add a Changelog entry with theme name, scope, and any known exceptions. |

> **Tip:** The Stage 2-2 Notion page includes a fully worked example (Founding Day) with exact steps and decisions. Read it before adding your first theme. The page also lists the 24 themable tokens with their Light + Dark values.

### Anti-patterns (Don't do this)

These are the mistakes that break the design system. Each one was a real issue in Safqah v1 or a known industry pitfall. Avoid them.

> **Don't:** Don't use primitive colors directly in product UI. If you reference Color/Primary/LightGreen/500 in a component, it won't update when a theme switches. Always use a semantic token like bg/brand/primary instead.

> **Don't:** Don't pair text/brand/primary with bg/surface or bg/base without a visible border/underline/icon. The contrast fails AA Normal. If you want green text on white, use text/brand/darkest instead - it passes.

> **Don't:** Don't use text/brand/primary or text/brand/darkest on bg/brand/yellow. Green-on-yellow combinations fail WCAG and look muddy. Yellow surfaces use text/default for content text.

> **Don't:** Don't use button labels below 14px Bold or 18px Regular on filled brand backgrounds. The white-on-brand contrast only passes AA Large at those weights. Smaller or lighter text fails WCAG.

> **Don't:** Don't modify existing primitive values to create a theme. That's how v1 broke - Founding Day overwrote Color/Primary/LightGreen/500 to a brown value, which silently changed every component everywhere. New themes create new primitives.

> **Don't:** Don't add modes to Primitive Core or Primitive / Typography. Modes belong on the Semantic collection. Adding modes to Primitives violates the locked-primitives rule and breaks the architectural contract.

> **Don't:** Don't use status colors for branding. text/success is for success messages - not for "this is positive in general." If you want brand-positive text on a neutral surface, use text/brand/darkest. Status meanings stay status meanings.
